lines.note: Section 1 of the GIC mechanism animation. Over the electrojet and the ground field. The number is measured at Ottawa.
lines.text: A hundred kilometres up, a sheet of current the width of a continent shifts south and strengthens. At Ottawa the magnetic field moved four hundred and thirty five nanotesla in one minute. On a quiet night it moves one.

lines.note: Section 2. Over Faraday's law and the induced E field in the ground. The point is rate, not depth.
lines.text: A magnetic field that changes drives an electric field in the rock beneath it. Faraday's law has a time derivative in it, so what matters is the rate and not the depth. A few volts per kilometre.

lines.note: Section 3. Over the transmission line with both neutrals grounded.
lines.text: Both ends of a long transmission line are bolted to the ground through a transformer neutral. Multiply a few volts per kilometre by a few hundred kilometres, and current flows up one neutral, along the line, and down the other.

lines.note: Section 4. Over the B-H curve with the DC offset pushing one half cycle over the knee.
lines.text: That current is nearly direct, and a core built for sixty hertz has no answer to it. The offset pushes half of every cycle over the knee, where a small change in flux costs an enormous magnetising current.

lines.note: Section 5. Over the harmonic spectrum and the heating transformer tank.
lines.text: The current stops being a sine wave and becomes a spike. A spike is a stack of harmonics the network was tuned to exclude, and the flux that no longer fits inside the core goes into the steel around it as heat.

lines.note: Section 6. Over the seven static compensators tripping in turn.
lines.text: The protective relays saw distortion they were built to disconnect for, and they disconnected. Seven compensators tripped one after another, inside a minute.

lines.note: Section 7. Over the voltage collapse and the ninety-two second clock.
lines.text: Five lines opened and the La Grande corridor was gone. Ninety two seconds later so was Quebec. Twenty one thousand five hundred megawatts, six million people, nine hours.
